title: Leadership Lessons from Special Agent Dale Cooper: What Twin Peaks Can Teach Us About School and Trust Leadership
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Using Twin Peaks' Special Agent Dale Cooper as an unlikely leadership case study, Hughes draws six lessons for school and trust leaders: leading with curiosity rather than premature certainty, balancing data patterns with attention to individuals, modelling calm because emotional tone is contagious, building trust through consistency and integrity, holding both evidence and professional instinct together, and recognising leadership is not the same as having all the answers. Her most concrete illustration is a student's account of a colleague deemed by leaders to be 'not deploying techniques properly', who was nonetheless called an 'icon' by pupils for their genuine subject passion - used to warn against reducing teaching quality to checklist compliance. She argues trust leaders in particular need this blend of rigour and humanity, since they must interpret data intelligently while still leaning on relational and local knowledge that no dashboard can capture.
points: Hughes's central device - drawing serious leadership lessons from a fictional detective - makes abstract leadership qualities (curiosity, calm, integrity) memorable through a shared cultural reference point.

Her anecdote about a teacher labelled as 'not deploying techniques properly' by leaders, yet called an 'icon' by students for genuine subject passion, is a concrete, vivid warning against checklist-driven teacher evaluation.
She explicitly argues that 'calm is contagious' in schools, framing a leader's emotional tone during inspection or crisis pressure as a deliberate leadership lever, not an incidental trait.
Her closing claim that leadership 'is not about having all the answers' reframes humility as strength rather than as a gap in leadership credibility.
quotes: Cooper is not a conventional leader. He is curious rather than arrogant, calm rather than theatrical, and deeply observant rather than controlling. He leads through presence, integrity, and trust-building.
Leadership becomes shallow when people are reduced to data points. Great school leaders know that behind every line on a spreadsheet is a child, a teacher, a family, or a colleague.

They told me about a colleague who they found inspirational... They even went so far as to call them an icon. Interestingly, this is a colleague who leaders had told me wasn't deploying techniques properly.
When leaders become reactive, agitated, or inconsistent, that anxiety spreads quickly across a staff team. When leaders remain calm, clear, and grounded, they create psychological safety.

The most credible leaders are often those who can say, We do not fully know yet, but we are paying attention, asking the right questions, and acting with care. In education, where the stakes are high and the terrain is complex, humility is not a weakness. It is a strength.
